records.question: What were the six-month survival percentages for Bruguiera gymnorrhiza and Rhizophora mangle saplings in the Nu'uuli restoration project?
records.ground_truth_answer: Bruguiera gymnorrhiza: 45% survival; Rhizophora mangle: 21% survival (six months after restoration).
ground_truth_chunks: While several years of monitoring may ultimately be required to determine the project's success, and several decades could be required to fully return the full suite of functions, the project's low-cost, nontechnical restoration techniques, using readily available materials, have proven to be modestly successful, with 38% sapling survival after six months.

Six months after initial restoration activities, there was a highly significant difference between Bruguiera gymnorrhiza and Rhizophora mangle sapling survival, with 21% and 45% of the original 42 R. mangle and 95 B. gymnorrhiza saplings remaining, respectively.

records.question: Why did the project decide not to raise mangrove saplings in a nursery and instead collect and transplant saplings from wild sources?
records.ground_truth_answer: They avoided raising seedlings in a nursery because nursery conditions (hydrologic regime, wave energy, salinity, nutrient levels, sun exposure) likely differ from the project site and thus ‘risks causing stress and low survivorship’ when transplanting. Collecting from the wild was preferred because saplings can be collected any time of year, are suitable for higher-energy sites, and usually have higher success rates than planting seeds.
ground_truth_chunks: We also decided not to raise saplings from seedlings in a nursery. Raising the seedlings in a nursery risks causing stress and low survivorship when transplanting to the project site, as conditions (e.g., hydrologic regime, wave energy, salinity, nutrient levels, sun exposure) in the nursery versus the project site are likely to differ.

Advantages of collection from the wild and transplanting are: saplings can be collected at any time through the year, they are suitable for higher energy sites, and success rates are usually higher than planting seeds.
